title: 使至塞上
titleEn: On a Mission to the Frontier
author: 王维
intro: An envoy rides out alone into the northwestern desert. The poem’s central couplet — a single column of smoke standing straight, a round sun setting over a long river — is perhaps the most famous desert image in Chinese.
analysis: 公元737年，王维奉命出使边塞，慰问打了胜仗的将士。开头说自己轻车简从去边疆，路过居延。接着诗人把自己比作随风飘飞的“征蓬”和北飞的“归雁”，暗含被排挤出朝廷的失落。第三联是千古名句：“大漠孤烟直，长河落日圆。”一望无际的沙漠上，一缕烟直直升起；长长的河上，一轮落日又大又圆。“直”和“圆”两个字简单得像几何线条，却画出了沙漠的辽阔和壮美，《红楼梦》里的香菱就说这两个字“似无理的，想去却是再找不出两个字换这两个来的”。最后写到了萧关，遇见侦察的骑兵，得知主帅还在前线。全诗由孤独转向壮阔，景象雄浑。
analysisEn: In 737 Wang Wei was sent from the capital to the northwestern frontier to bring the emperor’s congratulations to an army that had just defeated the Tibetans. He begins plainly: a light carriage, a few attendants, a long road past Juyan. Then he compares himself to tumbleweed blown out beyond the Han passes and to a wild goose flying north into foreign skies — images of drifting, with a hint that he has been pushed out of court. The third couplet is the one everyone knows: over the vast desert a lone column of smoke rises straight; over the long river the setting sun is round. The two key words, 直 (straight) and 圆 (round), are as simple as lines in a geometry book, yet they capture the emptiness and grandeur of the desert — with no wind and nothing in the way, smoke goes straight up; with nothing on the horizon, the sun looks huge and perfectly round. In the novel Dream of the Red Chamber, a girl learning poetry says these two words seem illogical, yet no other words could replace them. The poem ends at Xiao Pass, where a scout tells him the commander is still at the front.
background: Wang Wei (701–761) wrote this in 737, when he was sent as an imperial envoy to the Hexi frontier. The mission came soon after his patron Zhang Jiuling lost power, so many readers see it as a polite form of exile.
pronunciation: 候骑 hòu jì（统编教材注 jì，指骑马的人；今天“骑马”读 qí）。属国 shǔ guó（不读 zhǔ）。燕然 Yān rán（不读 yàn）。都护 dū hù（不读 dōu）。单车 dān chē。
version: 采用通行的教材版本，与《全唐诗》文本一致。“长河”一般解释为黄河，也有学者认为指当地的河流，解析里不展开。

lines.lit: With a single carriage I go to inquire at the frontier;
lines.en: With one light carriage I set out to visit the frontier,
an envoy on the long road past Juyan.

lines.lit: Drifting tumbleweed leaves the Han passes;
lines.en: Like tumbleweed I blow out past the Han passes,

lines.lit: returning geese enter the foreign sky.
lines.en: like a homing goose I enter the nomads’ sky.

lines.lit: In the great desert, a lone smoke is straight;
lines.en: On the endless desert one thread of smoke stands straight;

lines.lit: over the long river, the setting sun is round.
lines.en: over the long river the setting sun hangs round.

lines.lit: At Xiao Pass I meet a mounted scout:
lines.en: At Xiao Pass I meet a scout on horseback:

lines.lit: the commander is at Mount Yanran.
lines.en: “The commander is far ahead, at the front.”

words.note: 古义；今天“大使”“使者”还保留这个意思。
今天“单车”在南方口语里指自行车，意思完全不同。

words.en: to visit the frontier (to bring greetings)
envoy (an official title); here the poet himself
words.note: 古代官名“典属国”的简称。

words.en: Juyan, a frontier place in today’s Inner Mongolia

words.note: 蓬草枯了随风飘，常比喻漂泊的人。

words.en: the sky over the nomads’ lands
words.note: 胡：古代对北方、西方民族的称呼。
现代汉语也用，如“大漠风光”。
一般认为是报平安的烽烟，也有人说是炊烟或旋风卷起的沙尘。

words.en: the long river (usually taken as the Yellow River)

words.note: 骑：古代读 jì，指骑马的人；今天读 qí。
唐代边疆的最高军事长官。

words.en: Mount Yanran (in today’s Mongolia); here, the front line
words.note: 东汉窦宪曾在燕然山刻石记功，这里代指前线。

imagery.name: 雁
imagery.zh: 诗人把自己比作北飞的“归雁”，飞进陌生的边塞天空，带着漂泊和失落。
imagery.en: The poet sees himself as a goose flying north into a strange sky — drifting and a little lost.

imagery.name: 关
imagery.zh: “汉塞”“萧关”标出从内地走向边疆的路线。
imagery.en: The Han passes and Xiao Pass mark the road from China proper out to the frontier.

imagery.name: 烽火
imagery.zh: “孤烟”一般理解为报平安的烽烟，在无风的沙漠里笔直上升。
imagery.en: The lone smoke is usually read as a beacon signalling “all is well”, rising straight in the windless desert.

imagery.name: 夕阳
imagery.zh: 长河上又大又圆的落日，画出沙漠的辽阔与壮美。
imagery.en: The huge, round sun setting over the long river conveys the vastness and grandeur of the desert.
